V01.answer: Yes, you should report in. Canggu's customary village rules (awig-awig) treat anyone who isn't a registered member as a tamiu, a guest, and a non-Hindu guest who is staying here and making a living is expected to report to the village/banjar officials within one wuku (seven days) with clear documents, then pay a monthly sadana krama contribution. For a two-month rental, that means planning to register rather than just settling in quietly. The exact amount, paperwork and which office you go to are decided locally by each banjar, so your landlord or host is the quickest way to get it right.
V01.why_it_matters: Reporting and contributing is how guests are folded into village life here, so the banjar knows who is around and can include you in neighbourhood matters and ceremonies.
recommended_actions: Ask your landlord or host which banjar your rental falls under and how to report
Go to the village or banjar officials within your first week with your passport and rental agreement
Ask what the monthly sadana krama contribution is and how it is paid
Introduce yourself to your immediate neighbours so they know who is living there

V01.search_translation: Aku menyewa rumah di Canggu selama dua bulan. Apa aku harus melapor ke banjar?

V02.answer: Ya, sebaiknya Anda melapor. Menurut aturan adat Desa Adat Canggu (awig-awig), pendatang yang bukan warga adat tergolong tamiu, dan tamiu diminta melapor ke prajuru dalam satu wuku, sekitar tujuh hari, dengan dokumen yang jelas. Kalau Anda bukan Hindu, laporannya ke prajuru dinas; kalau Hindu, ke prajuru adat dan dinas. Anda juga akan diminta membayar sadana krama, iuran keanggotaan, yang besarnya ditetapkan masing-masing banjar (dewan lingkungan setempat). Karena itu ketentuan detailnya bisa berbeda antar banjar, jadi tanyakan langsung ke banjar di lingkungan Anda.
V02.why_it_matters: Melapor membuat banjar mengenal siapa saja yang tinggal di wilayahnya, sehingga Anda lebih mudah diterima dan ikut serta dalam kehidupan bersama di lingkungan.
recommended_actions: Lapor ke prajuru desa atau banjar setempat dalam satu wuku sejak Anda mulai tinggal.
Bawa dokumen identitas dan keterangan tempat tinggal yang jelas saat melapor.
Tanyakan ke banjar besaran sadana krama dan cara pembayarannya.

V03.answer: Sort your rubbish at the villa into separate containers by type, rather than putting everything in one bag. Canggu's customary village rules ask every household, including guests, to limit single-use plastic, choose recyclable or easily compostable packaging, and keep five kinds of waste storage for separated waste. Inorganic waste that can be sold should go to the shared village waste unit or your banjar's waste group on their set schedule; non-sellable inorganic and leftover residual waste go in the designated place for village collection. Ask your host or villa staff how the bins are arranged and when collection happens.
V03.why_it_matters: Keeping waste separate is part of a shared neighbourhood effort, so Canggu's customary village can keep public lanes, beaches and waterways clean for everyone.
recommended_actions: Set up separate bins or bags for different waste types at your villa
Avoid single-use plastic and choose recyclable or easily compostable packaging
Take sellable inorganic waste to the shared waste unit or neighbourhood waste group on their schedule
Ask your host or local banjar for the collection schedule and how your villa should handle residual waste

Pasal 6 Pengelolaan Sampah Rumah Tangga
(1) Setiap Krama Adat, Krama Tamiu, dan Tamiu dalam rumah tangga wajib melakukan pengelolaan sampah yang dihasilkannya.
(2) Pengelolaan sampah rumah tangga sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1) dilakukan dengan cara: a. menggunakan barang dan/atau kemasan yang dapat didaur ulang dan mudah terurai oleh proses alam; b. membatasi timbulan sampah dengan tidak menggunakan plastik sekali pakai; c. menyediakan 5 (lima) jenis tempat penyimpanan sampah yang layak untuk menyimpan sampah terpilah berdasarkan jenisnya; d. melakukan pemilahan dan pewadahan sampah berdasarkan jenisnya; e. menyerahkan sampah jenis an-organik yang memiliki nilai jual ke unit pengelola sampah bersama dan/atau ke pengurus sekaa resik di tiap banjar adat sesuai dengan jadwal yang telah ditentukan; f. menempatkan sampah jenis an-organik yang tidak memiliki nilai jual dan sampah residu pada tempatnya, yang selanjutnya akan diambil oleh petugas unit pengelola sampah bersama tingkat desa.

V04.answer: Ya, sampah rumah tangga di Canggu memang harus dipilah, dan aturan desa adat setempat berlaku juga untuk pendatang yang tinggal di sini. Intinya tiga hal: kurangi plastik sekali pakai dan pilih kemasan yang bisa didaur ulang atau mudah terurai; pilah sampah ke wadah terpisah menurut jenisnya, aturan setempat menyebut lima jenis wadah; lalu serahkan sampah anorganik yang masih bernilai jual ke pengelola sampah bersama atau pengurus kebersihan di banjar Anda sesuai jadwal, sementara sampah anorganik tanpa nilai jual dan sampah residu ditaruh di tempatnya untuk diambil petugas desa. Kalau jadwal dan jenis pemilahannya belum jelas, tanyakan ke pengurus banjar atau host akomodasi Anda.
V04.why_it_matters: Sampah di sini dianggap urusan bersama, dan aturan desa adat menempatkan setiap rumah tangga, termasuk pendatang, sebagai bagian dari tanggung jawab menjaga kebersihan lingkungan Canggu.

Kurangi plastik sekali pakai dan pilih kemasan yang mudah terurai atau bisa didaur ulang
Antar sampah anorganik bernilai jual ke pengelola sampah bersama atau pengurus kebersihan banjar sesuai jadwal
Tanyakan ke pengurus banjar atau host soal lima jenis wadah dan jadwal penyerahan setempat

V04.search_translation: How do you sort out household garbage in the Incant?

V05.answer: Yes — under Canggu's customary village rules (awig-awig / pararem), sorting your rubbish is your responsibility, and that covers visitors and newcomers, not only registered villagers. If you don't separate your waste properly, the village's waste service can simply stop collecting from you. Repeat or serious breaches can move to a formal warning and then to a customary sanction decided by the village officials — a fine set somewhere between the price of 10 and 100 kg of premium rice, a day spent cleaning public areas, or a purification ceremony. The exact penalty is decided case by case by the banjar (the neighbourhood council), so no fixed figure applies in advance.
V05.why_it_matters: Rubbish in rivers, drains, roads and temple verges affects everyone who lives and worships here, so keeping waste in order is treated as a shared duty rather than a private habit.
recommended_actions: Separate your waste at home before putting it out for collection.
Take rubbish to designated collection points instead of drains, rivers, roads, beaches or temple verges.
Avoid burning rubbish yourself without the village officials' approval.
Ask your host or the local banjar how collection works on your street.

V05.search_translation: Apa yang terjadi jika aku tidak memisahkan sampahku di Canggu? Apakah ada sanksi?

V06.answer: Sebaiknya Anda menghindari empat hal ini selama Nyepi: menyalakan api atau lampu terang, bekerja, bepergian keluar, dan membuat suara keras atau bersenang-senang. Ini disebut catur brata penyepian, bagian dari aturan desa adat Canggu (awig-awig). Aturan itu ditulis untuk warga adat setempat, tetapi di praktiknya seluruh lingkungan ikut hening, jadi sebagai tamu cara paling sopan adalah ikut tenang di dalam ruangan, mengurangi lampu dan suara, serta tidak berkendara di hari itu. Pengecualian diberikan untuk hal mendesak, misalnya merawat bayi di bawah tiga bulan atau orang sakit di rumah.
V06.why_it_matters: Nyepi adalah hari hening yang penting bagi warga Bali, dan ikut menjaga ketenangan adalah cara paling tulus untuk menghormati tuan rumah tempat Anda menginap.
recommended_actions: Tetap di dalam ruangan dan jaga suasana tenang sepanjang hari Nyepi
Kurangi atau matikan lampu terang dan hindari musik atau suara keras
Jangan bepergian atau berkendara di jalan selama Nyepi
Tanyakan ke pengelola akomodasi soal kebutuhan mendesak atau izin khusus

(3) Hari setelah Nyepi disebut Ngembak Geni, yang berarti berakhirnya yoga semadi, disertai saling memaafkan antar-krama desa/banjar sebagai tanda awal Tahun Saka.

Ask before taking photos, especially of people praying or during a ceremony

Canang sari are the small offerings Balinese Hindus place every day near homes, shops, shrines and on the ground, and they're part of daily worship, not decoration or litter. So if you see one on a pavement or by a doorway, step around it when you can, and if you're not sure what something is or where it was placed, just ask your host or a local guide. Don't move, kick or disturb them.
V10.why_it_matters: These offerings are a small but essential part of everyday devotion here, so treating them with care is a simple sign of respect for the people around you.

V11.answer: Galungan and Kuningan are two of the most important celebrations in Balinese Hindu religious life. They mark devotion to God and the victory of dharma, goodness, over adharma, evil. They are genuine religious occasions, not a festival put on for visitors, so what you'll notice around Canggu is real preparation and worship: penjor (the tall decorated bamboo poles) outside homes, offerings being made, processions, and sometimes shops or roads running differently for a while. If you come across a ceremony, watch quietly from a respectful distance rather than stepping in, and ask your host or a local guide what's appropriate. It's also worth remembering that villages don't all celebrate in exactly the same way.
V11.why_it_matters: These days are about devotion and the triumph of good over evil, so treating them with quiet respect means a lot to the Balinese families and neighbours around you.
recommended_actions: Ask your host or a local guide what is appropriate if you encounter a ceremony
Observe from an appropriate place without disrupting worship
Respect temporary changes to access, traffic or opening hours around religious days
Check a current Balinese calendar for this year's dates rather than assuming a fixed day

V13.answer: Yes to the helmet, and yes to being properly licensed — the two go together here. Bali's provincial rules, including a 2025 governor's circular, require anyone riding to wear a properly fastened helmet, follow signs and passenger limits, and never ride after drinking. Foreign visitors driving in Bali also need a valid national or international driving licence that matches the vehicle, along with the vehicle documents, and should rent from a properly registered business. A short, quiet ride doesn't make any of this optional. One thing worth checking: the same circular points foreign tourists towards four-wheeled transport from registered rental businesses, so ask your rental provider what applies to scooters.
V13.why_it_matters: Helmets and valid licences are how people here keep very busy, shared roads safe for riders, passengers and pedestrians alike.
recommended_actions: Wear a properly fastened helmet on every ride, however short
Carry a valid national or international driving licence plus the vehicle documents
Rent from a properly registered rental business and check the bike is roadworthy
Ask your rental provider or host which vehicles foreign visitors may legally use here

V16.answer: Yes, walking and cycling are normal ways to get around Canggu, but you need to stay alert rather than assume it's set up for it. Sidewalks come and go, and a quiet-looking road isn't automatically a safe one. Where there's a footpath, use it; where there isn't, keep your eyes open and follow the road rules instead of treating the road edge as your own lane. On a bike, ride predictably, keep to the correct side, use lights in poor visibility and wear a helmet. And please don't leave bikes or yourself blocking village roads, temple access, shop entrances or emergency access.
V16.why_it_matters: These streets are shared by residents, businesses, delivery riders and visitors, so moving considerately keeps access open and reduces avoidable risk for everyone.

V19.answer: No — please don't. Both Bali's provincial rules and Canggu's customary village rules (the awig-awig and pararem made by the banjar, the neighbourhood council) say nobody may throw rubbish, waste or sewage into a river, spring, lake, drain or the sea. Burning or dumping rubbish in the open is off the list too. The same rules ask everyone to keep waste out of the lanes, the telajakan (the planted strip in front of a property), and any spot that isn't a proper bin. For you as a visitor, it simply means carrying your rubbish until you find a bin or a collection point, and keeping the beaches and rivers here clean for the people who live from them and pray near them.
V19.why_it_matters: Water and land are sacred to Balinese communities and the island's rivers and coastline are also how many families here earn a living, so keeping them clean is treated as a shared duty.
recommended_actions: Carry your rubbish with you until you find a bin or collection point
Keep waste out of rivers, drains, the sea, lanes and planted verges
Ask your accommodation host where to leave waste if you are unsure
Report any dumping or burning you notice to your host or the local banjar

H04.answer: Ya, usaha restoran Anda termasuk yang diatur. Sebagai pemilik usaha di Canggu, Anda wajib mengelola sampah sendiri dengan baik, terutama saat berada di area publik seperti jalan, telajakan, selokan, dan pantai. Desa adat hanya menangani sampah di area publik yang tidak dikelola secara khusus, jadi jangan mengandalkan membuang sampah usaha ke sana. Usaha juga dilibatkan dalam gotong royong kebersihan yang diadakan berkala, setidaknya sebulan sekali. Sanksinya bersifat praktis: kalau sampah tidak dipilah dengan baik, unit pengelola sampah desa tidak akan mengangkut sampah Anda. Pihak desa adat sendiri bertugas mengedukasi dan mengawasi usaha-usaha di wilayahnya.

H05.answer: You drive on the left here, so keep left and go with the flow of traffic. Signal before you turn or change direction, and give pedestrians and cyclists a bit of room, especially on narrow roads around Canggu. Parking is the other thing to watch: use spots where it's clearly permitted and don't block traffic or a pedestrian path. If you're riding a scooter, wear a properly fastened helmet, sort out a valid licence, and pull over safely if you need to check your phone. It's really about being predictable so everyone can read what you'll do next.
H05.why_it_matters: On Bali's narrow, busy roads, driving predictably and giving way to the more vulnerable people around you keeps things calm and safe for everyone, visitors and locals alike.
recommended_actions: Keep to the left side of the road and follow signs, markings and police directions
Signal before turning or changing lanes
Park only where permitted, without blocking traffic or footpaths
Pull over safely before using your phone, and keep your helmet fastened on a scooter

H06.answer: No, better not ride at all after drinking. Bali's provincial rules for foreign visitors are clear that you must not drive under the influence of alcohol or illegal drugs, and a short ride or a quiet road doesn't make the safety rules optional. If you're renting a scooter, you also need a valid licence for that vehicle and a properly registered rental, and you should wear a fastened helmet and stay within the passenger limit. Plan ahead instead: walk, or use a driver or ride-hailing car on nights when you've been drinking.
H06.why_it_matters: Road safety here protects not only you but also passengers, pedestrians and everyone else sharing narrow, busy roads where traffic is unpredictable.
recommended_actions: Skip the scooter entirely if you've been drinking and arrange a driver, ride-hailing car or a walk home instead
Only ride with a valid licence recognised in Indonesia, a helmet fastened properly and a registered rental vehicle
Follow signs, signals and police directions, and stop safely before checking your phone for navigation

H08.answer: Tri Hita Karana is a Balinese way of describing three relationships that keep life in balance: Parahyangan, the tie between people and the divine; Pawongan, the ties among people; and Palemahan, the tie between people and the environment. It isn't a rulebook or a checklist you have to tick off. It's a broad lens people here use to talk about why temples, neighbours and the land all matter together. For you as a newcomer, it's a helpful way to understand why a shrine in a rice field or a shared clean-up feels significant. It's general cultural guidance, not a law, and villages and families may explain it differently, so it's worth asking people locally how they see it.
H08.why_it_matters: Seeing your street, its temples and its people as connected helps explain why small acts of care and courtesy are noticed and appreciated here.
recommended_actions: Treat the three dimensions as a broad way of understanding local life rather than a complete explanation of every practice.
Ask a local guide, neighbour or community representative how the concept is understood in your area.
Notice how shrines, neighbours and shared spaces sit together in daily life, and act with care in each.
